To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the performance and cost of cloud services are highly workload-dependent; (2) the cost and performance are significantly different depending on the architecture of the cloud service; and (3) there is no clear-cut winner among the cloud vendors.

the following question: what is the best architecture for transaction processing in a cloud computing setting?
understanding the impact of the architectural decisions that are taken in cloud computing services.
the evaluation of the performance and cost of cloud computing services for transaction processing applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single best architecture, and that the choice depends on the workload characteristics and the application requirements.
there is no one-size-fits-all architecture that is best for all workloads.
the state of the art in commercial cloud services is not yet ready to support data-intensive workloads.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cloud computing is a very good option for data intensive applications if the workload is read-only, but that there is no clear winner for transaction processing workloads.
there is no single architecture for the cloud that works for all workloads and all vendors.
the cloud computing model has not yet reached maturity for transaction processing workloads.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the architecture of the cloud service is a key determinant of the performance and cost for database applications.
the architecture matters, and the cost and performance implications of different architectures should be understood by the application designer.
the cloud services are not a panacea for transaction processing.
